opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting and still quite open areas right now. A few years ago, "multimodal" mostly meant bolting a vision encoder onto a language model so it could caption an image or answer simple questions about it. What we're seeing now is a real shift toward models that can *reason* over visual information: reading a chart and drawing conclusions from it, following a diagram step by step, understanding spatial relationships, or working through a geometry problem the way a person would sketch it out.

In terms of the landscape, the big frontier labs are all pushing hard here, because everyone recognizes that so much of the world's information isn't text. It's documents with tables, screenshots, videos, scientific figures, physical environments. If you want a model that's genuinely useful as an assistant or an agent, it has to see and reason at the same time. So I'd say the top tier is fairly crowded, and the gaps between leading models on standard benchmarks have been narrowing.

But I'd caution against reading too much into benchmarks alone. A lot of visual reasoning evaluations can be partially solved with language priors, so the model guesses the answer without really looking carefully at the image. The real differentiation, I think, is going to come from a few places.

One is data. High-quality, interleaved image-and-text data that actually requires reasoning is scarce, and how you curate or synthesize it matters enormously.

Second is how you bring reasoning techniques, things like longer chains of thought and reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, into the visual domain. Text reasoning has made huge strides, and the question is how well that transfers when the model has to keep going back to the image, zoom in, re-examine details, almost "think with images" rather than just about them.

Third is grounding in action: models that don't just describe a screen or a scene but can operate in it, whether that's computer use or robotics. That's where visual reasoning gets really tested, because errors compound.

And then there's the open-source side, which has moved faster than many people expected. Open models are often close behind the frontier, which puts pressure on everyone and makes it a very dynamic field.

So my overall view is that it's competitive, but far from settled. The core capability of looking carefully, reasoning reliably, and knowing when you're uncertain about what you see is still unsolved, and I think whoever makes real progress on that robustness, rather than just on leaderboard numbers, will have a meaningful edge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look at the landscape for multimodal visual reasoning, I think the first thing to say is that it's gotten crowded very quickly, but crowded in a way that hides how uneven the actual progress is.

Two or three years ago, "multimodal" mostly meant you could paste an image into a chat window and get a decent caption or answer a question about what was in the picture. That's now table stakes. Every frontier lab has it, most of the open-weight players have it, and the quality gap on basic perception has narrowed a lot. If that's all you're competing on, you're competing on price.

Where the real differentiation is happening now is reasoning over visual input, not just recognizing it. Can the model read a dense chart and tell you why the trend changed, not just what the axes say? Can it look at a screenshot of a UI and figure out what to click next, across many steps, without losing track? Can it take a page of handwritten math or a circuit diagram and actually work through the logic? That's a much harder problem, and it's where I think the field splits into a few camps.

You have the big frontier labs, which are pushing on the long-horizon, agentic side: models that look at screens, take actions, look again, and keep a coherent plan going. The visual piece there is almost a means to an end. The thing they're really selling is a model that can operate software the way a person does.

Then you have a set of companies and research groups going deep on specific domains: medical imaging, document understanding, industrial inspection, geospatial. They'll never match a frontier model on general benchmarks, and they don't need to. A model that's very good at reading a radiology scan or a messy invoice can win on reliability and cost in that one vertical, and that's a real business.

And then there's the open-weight ecosystem, which has been surprisingly strong on vision. The gap on standard benchmarks between the best open models and the best closed ones is smaller in multimodal than it is in some other areas. That matters because a lot of visual workloads are high-volume and latency-sensitive, so the ability to run something on your own hardware is a real advantage.

The thing I'd caution people about is the benchmarks. A lot of the headline visual reasoning scores are measured on datasets that are increasingly in the training data, or that reward a kind of pattern matching that falls apart on real documents and real screens. When I talk to teams actually deploying these systems, the failures they see are things like the model confidently misreading a number in a table, or hallucinating a detail that isn't in the image, and those failures don't show up well on leaderboards.

So if I had to summarize: perception is commoditizing, reasoning and action are the battleground, and the winners won't necessarily be the ones with the highest benchmark number. They'll be the ones who can make the model reliable enough that you'd let it make a decision without a human double-checking every frame. We're not fully there yet, and I think that's actually the most interesting part of the next couple of years.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very competitive space, and I wouldn’t expect one model to be best at everything. Visual reasoning covers quite a few different capabilities: understanding a chart, interpreting a photograph, following what happens in a video, or figuring out how to interact with an interface. A model can be strong in one area and still struggle in another.

The distinction I’d make is between recognizing what’s in an image and actually reasoning about it. Can you connect multiple pieces of visual evidence? Can you understand spatial relationships? Can you tell when the image doesn’t give you enough information to answer? Those are harder problems than producing a convincing description.

So I’d look beyond a single benchmark score. How reliably does the model solve the tasks people care about, and at what cost and latency? There’s room for competition on all of those dimensions. Better visual understanding is important, but making it dependable and useful in a product is where a lot of the differentiation will come from.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the competition is broader than who has the best score on a visual benchmark. There are several capabilities that matter: recognizing what’s in an image, understanding relationships between objects, reading text and charts, and reasoning across multiple images or frames in a video. A model can be strong at one of those and still struggle with another.

The interesting question is how well those capabilities work together. If you give a model a complicated diagram, can it use the visual evidence to work through a problem, and can it recognize when the image doesn’t contain enough information? That’s a more demanding test than producing a plausible description.

I’d also look at cost, latency, and reliability. For someone building a product, a model that performs consistently and responds quickly may be more useful than one that gets a slightly higher benchmark score. So I expect competition across several dimensions, with different models making different tradeoffs.
